prompt.text:
Your task is to generate a complete research paper using the materials below.
You must produce:
1. A BibTeX bibliography file (references.bib)
2. The full LaTeX paper (template.tex)

Instructions
• Use the research idea and experimental logs to construct a coherent, rigorous ML paper.
• For related work and baselines:
  – Search for and include influential papers published up until 2024-11.
  – Incorporate relevant literature and add the corresponding BibTeX entries to references.bib.
  – Do NOT hallucinate papers or reference keys; all citation entries must be real.
• In the LaTeX paper, cite papers using \cite{} with keys that match exactly with your entries in references.bib.
• Do not fabricate experimental results or make claims unsupported by the logs.

Materials
Here are all the raw research materials to assist with the writing process:

[RESEARCH IDEA]
## Problem Statement

The deployment of Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) in safety-critical domains is currently hindered by their vulnerability to adversarial perturbations. While "complete" verification methods (which provide exact guarantees) are computationally intractable (NP-complete) for large networks, "incomplete" methods (which rely on linear relaxation) offer scalability at the cost of precision. A significant bottleneck in current incomplete verifiers is the handling of the **MaxPool** layer.

Existing techniques for verifying MaxPool-based networks suffer from a dichotomy: they either use coarse linear approximations that introduce excessive error (over-approximation) or they transform MaxPool layers into sequences of ReLUs, which drastically increases computational complexity. Furthermore, recent attempts to tighten these bounds focus on "block-wise" tightness (combining ReLU and MaxPool), which becomes sub-optimal when the ReLU layers are already handled by high-precision Branch-and-Bound (BaB) techniques. There is currently no method that provides the provably tightest linear approximation specifically for the multivariate MaxPool neuron itself, leading to unnecessary precision loss during robustness certification.

## Core Hypothesis

We propose that the verification precision of MaxPool-based CNNs can be significantly improved without sacrificing efficiency by deriving the **neuron-wise tightest linear bounds** for the MaxPool function.

Our core intuition is that the MaxPool function, being piece-wise linear, has a specific geometric structure over a bounded input domain. We hypothesize that by explicitly minimizing the volume of the "over-approximation zone"—the space between the true non-linear function and its linear bounding planes—we can reduce the accumulation of error as it propagates through the network. We believe it is possible to mathematically prove that a specific configuration of linear planes (anchored at optimal points in the input space) constitutes the tightest possible linear relaxation for a MaxPool neuron.

## Proposed Methodology (High-Level Technical Approach)

We propose to develop a novel robustness verifier module designed to replace standard MaxPool relaxations in existing frameworks. The approach will focus on geometric analysis and volume minimization:

1.  **Geometric Analysis of the Input Domain:**
    We will treat the inputs to a MaxPool operation as a hypercube defined by the lower and upper bounds propagated from previous layers. We aim to analyze the geometry of the MaxPool surface within this constrained region.

2.  **Construction of Adaptive Linear Bounds:**
    *   **Upper Bound Strategy:** Instead of generic heuristics, we will construct an upper linear plane that passes through specific "anchor points" on the space diagonal of the input hypercube. By selecting coefficients based on the sorted order of the input bounds, we ensure the plane "hugs" the actual MaxPool function as closely as possible from above.
    *   **Lower Bound Strategy:** We will derive a lower linear plane that passes through the precise midpoint of the input region. This selection aims to maximize the volume underneath the plane while remaining a valid lower bound, thereby squeezing the over-approximation zone from the bottom.

3.  **Minimizing the Over-Approximation Integral:**
    We will formulate an optimization objective to minimize the integral of the difference between the upper and lower linear bounds. We intend to prove that our specific selection of planes (derived in step 2) yields the global minimum for this integral, thereby achieving "neuron-wise tightness."

4.  **Algorithmic Integration:**
    The implementation will be designed as a lightweight, plug-and-play component. It will determine the optimal linear coefficients dynamically by simply inspecting and sorting the pre-computed bounds of the incoming features. This allows integration into various verification paradigms, including back-substitution, multi-neuron relaxation, and branch-and-bound frameworks, without requiring complex solvers or layer transformations.

## Expected Contribution

*   **Theoretical Novelty:** We expect to provide the first theoretical proof for the neuron-wise tightest linear bounds of the multivariate MaxPool function. This fills a gap in the literature where focus has largely been on univariate activations (like Sigmoid) or block-combinations.
*   **Precision Improvement:** By minimizing the over-approximation zone at the neuron level, we anticipate a significant increase in certified accuracy (the percentage of inputs proven robust) compared to state-of-the-art baselines.
*   **Operational Efficiency:** Unlike methods that decompose MaxPool into complex sub-structures, our approach preserves the layer's native structure. We expect to achieve these tighter bounds with negligible computational overhead, maintaining the speed of the fastest existing linear verifiers.

[EXPERIMENTAL LOGS]
## 1. Experimental Setup

We implemented a neuron-wise tightest linear approximation method for MaxPool layers, termed Ti-Lin, and evaluated its performance by integrating it into existing verification frameworks.

*   **Datasets:**
    *   MNIST
    *   CIFAR-10
    *   Tiny ImageNet (mentioned in text analysis, though primary tabular results focus on MNIST/CIFAR/ModelNet40)
    *   ModelNet40 (for PointNet experiments)
*   **Evaluation Metrics:**
    *   **Certified Accuracy (%):** The percentage of instances verified as safe under perturbation.
    *   **Upper Bound (UB %):** Robustness verification upper bounds computed by PGD attacks.
    *   **Average Runtime:** Measured in seconds or minutes depending on the experiment.
    *   **Speedup:** Relative time improvement ($t_{baseline} / t_{Ti-Lin}$).
    *   **Timeout Rate (%):** Percentage of instances where verification timed out (specifically for BaB-based experiments).
*   **Baselines & Frameworks Compared:**
    *   **Backsubstitution-based:** DeepPoly, 3DCertify (built atop DeepPoly), CNN-Cert.
    *   **Multi-Neuron (MN) based:** ERAN, MN-BaB.
    *   **Branch and Bound (BaB) based:** $\alpha, \beta$-CROWN, MaxLin (integrated into $\alpha, \beta$-CROWN).
    *   **Other:** OSIP (referenced in text comparisons).
*   **Networks:**
    *   Conv_MaxPool, Convnet_MaxPool.
    *   CNNs with depths varying from 4 to 8 layers.
    *   PointNets (16p, 32p, 64p; Natural, FGSM-trained, IBP-trained).
*   **Implementation Details:**
    *   **Hardware:** Server with 48-core Intel Xeon Silver 4310 CPU and 125 GB RAM.
    *   **Timeout:** 180 seconds for general experiments; 3600 seconds for specific BaB experiments to allow thorough exploration.
    *   **Integration:** Ti-Lin was instantiated within the DeepPoly, ERAN, and $\alpha, \beta$-CROWN frameworks to ensure fair comparison against baselines within the same architecture.
    *   **Perturbation Norms:** Experiments covered $l_1, l_2,$ and $l_\infty$ norm perturbations.
    *   **Data conversions:** For Table 3, CNNs (4-8 layers) on MNIST and CIFAR-10 were converted from `.h5` to `.onnx` format.

## 3. Qualitative Observations

*   **Observation 1 (Linear Bounds Geometry):** We observed that the neuron-wise tightest upper linear bound for the MaxPool function is a plane passing through two endpoints of the space diagonal of the input region and the midpoint of the input region. The lower linear bound plane passes through the midpoint of the input region and satisfies $l(m) = f(m)$.
*   **Observation 2 (Bound Regions):** We identified four distinct cases for constructing the linear bounds depending on the relative values of the input interval bounds ($l_i, u_i$). Specifically, the coefficients of the linear bounds change based on which input variable bounds are maximal.
*   **Observation 3 (Comparison with DeepPoly/3DCertify):** Ti-Lin achieved higher certified accuracy across all settings when compared to DeepPoly and 3DCertify. Specifically, we recorded up to 39.4% improvement over DeepPoly and 7.1% over 3DCertify on the MNIST_CNN_8layers network.
*   **Observation 4 (Runtime Efficiency vs 3DCertify):** Ti-Lin demonstrated higher time efficiency than 3DCertify, with speedups up to 5.3x. This is attributed to Ti-Lin providing the best upper linear bound directly, whereas 3DCertify computes every possible upper linear bound to select the best one.
*   **Observation 5 (Comparison with ERAN/MN-BaB):** Ti-Lin outperformed MN-BaB and ERAN in certified accuracy across all networks, showing up to 39.4% improvement on MNIST_CNN_8layers.
*   **Observation 6 (Runtime vs MN-BaB):** While Ti-Lin was faster than MN-BaB on most MNIST networks, both Ti-Lin and ERAN were slower than MN-BaB on CIFAR-10 networks (up to 2.6x slowdown).
*   **Observation 7 (Comparison with $\alpha, \beta$-CROWN/MaxLin):** When integrated into the $\alpha, \beta$-CROWN framework, Ti-Lin improved certified accuracy by up to 78.6% compared to the baseline $\alpha, \beta$-CROWN and 28.6% compared to MaxLin (specifically on CIFAR_CNN_6layers).
*   **Observation 8 (Timeout Reduction):** Using Ti-Lin significantly reduced the timeout rate in BaB-based verification compared to baselines. For example, on CIFAR-10 CNN 6 layers, the timeout rate dropped from 92.9% ($\alpha, \beta$-CROWN) and 42.9% (MaxLin) to 15.3% (Ti-Lin).
*   **Observation 9 (Tightness Property):** We observed that MaxLin provides block-wise tightest bounds (effective when ReLU is bounded by a single upper constraint), whereas Ti-Lin provides neuron-wise tightest bounds, which achieved higher precision when ReLU is bounded by tighter constraints (BaB techniques).

prompt.text:
Role: Senior AI Researcher and Academic Writer.
Objective: Complete a machine learning research paper by filling in missing sections of a provided LaTeX template and generating a corresponding bibliography file. You must produce a scientifically sound, well-structured paper suitable for submission to a top-tier ML conference.

Inputs
You will receive the following materials:
• idea.md: Detailed description of the proposed method and technical ideas.
• experimental_log.md: Raw experimental results and observations used to construct tables, figures, and analysis.
• conference_guidelines.md: Formatting and stylistic requirements for the target conference.
• figures_list: A list of figures that may be referenced in the paper.

Conference Guidelines
# CVPR 2025 Paper Writing Guidelines

Below are the instructions to help you with the latex paper writing process for CVPR 2025.

## Language
All manuscripts must be in English.

## Submission Policies & Anonymity
CVPR reviewing is double-blind. Authors must not know the names of the reviewers, and reviewers must not know the names of the authors.

* **No Identifying Information:** Do not provide information that may identify the authors in the acknowledgments (e.g., co-workers and grant IDs) or in the supplementary material.
* **Links:** Do not provide links to websites that identify the authors.
* **GitHub:** Links to GitHub must be anonymous.
* **Self-Citation:** If you need to cite any of your own papers that are being submitted concurrently, include anonymized versions in the supplementary material and cite them as anonymous. Do not use the words "my" or "our" when citing previous work; treat your own prior work as if it were written by someone else (e.g., "Smith et al. showed..." rather than "We showed...").

## Paper length
Papers, excluding the references section, must be no longer than eight pages in length.
The references section will not be included in the page count, and there is no limit on the length of the references section.
For example, a paper of eight pages with two pages of references would have a total length of 10 pages.

Overlength papers, or papers where margins and formatting are deemed significantly altered, will simply not be reviewed.

## Mathematics
Please number all of your sections and displayed equations as in these examples:
```latex
\begin{equation}
  E = m\cdot c^2
  \label{eq:important}
\end{equation}
```
and
```latex
\begin{equation}
  v = a\cdot t.
  \label{eq:also-important}
\end{equation}
```

## Formatting your paper
All text must be in a two-column format.
The total allowable size of the text area is $6\frac78$ inches (17.46 cm) wide by $8\frac78$ inches (22.54 cm) high.
Columns are to be $3\frac14$ inches (8.25 cm) wide, with a $\frac{5}{16}$ inch (0.8 cm) space between them.
The main title (on the first page) should begin 1 inch (2.54 cm) from the top edge of the page.
The second and following pages should begin 1 inch (2.54 cm) from the top edge.
On all pages, the bottom margin should be $1\frac{1}{8}$ inches (2.86 cm) from the bottom edge of the page for $8.5 \times 11$-inch paper;
for A4 paper, approximately $1\frac{5}{8}$ inches (4.13 cm) from the bottom edge of the page.

### Type style and fonts
Wherever Times is specified, Times Roman may also be used. If neither is available on your word processor, please use the font closest in appearance to Times to which you have access.

### Main Title
Center the title $1\frac{3}{8}$ inches (3.49 cm) from the top edge of the first page. The title should be in Times 14-point, boldface type. Capitalize the first letter of nouns, pronouns, verbs, adjectives, and adverbs; do not capitalize articles, coordinate conjunctions, or prepositions (unless the title begins with such a word).

The ABSTRACT and MAIN TEXT are to be in a two-column format.

### Main Text
Type main text in 10-point Times, single-spaced.
Do NOT use double-spacing.
All paragraphs should be indented 1 pica (approx.~$\frac{1}{6}$ inch or 0.422 cm). Make sure your text is fully justified---that is, flush left and flush right. Please do not place any additional blank lines between paragraphs.

Figure and table captions should be 9-point Roman type as in \cref{fig:onecol,fig:short}. 
Short captions should be centred.

\noindent Callouts should be 9-point Helvetica, non-boldface type. Initially capitalize only the first word of section titles and first-, second-, and third-order headings.

#### First-order Headings
For example, {\large \bf 1. Introduction} should be Times 12-point boldface, initially capitalized, flush left, with one blank line before, and one blank line after.

#### Second-order Headings
For example, { \bf 1.1. Database elements} should be Times 11-point boldface, initially capitalized, flush left, with one blank line before, and one after.
If you require a third-order heading (we discourage it), use 10-point Times, boldface, initially capitalized, flush left, preceded by one blank line, followed by a period and your text on the same line.

### Footnotes
Please use \footnote{This is what a footnote looks like.
It often distracts the reader from the main flow of the argument.} sparingly.

Indeed, try to avoid footnotes altogether and include necessary peripheral observations in the text (within parentheses, if you prefer, as in this sentence). If you wish to use a footnote, place it at the bottom of the column on the page on which it is referenced.
Use Times 8-point type, single-spaced.

### Cross-references
For the benefit of author(s) and readers, please use the
```latex
{\small\begin{verbatim}
  \cref{...}
\end{verbatim}}
```
command for cross-referencing to figures, tables, equations, or sections.

This will automatically insert the appropriate label alongside the cross-reference as in this example:
```latex
\begin{quotation}
  To see how our method outperforms previous work, please see \cref{fig:onecol} and \cref{tab:example}.
  It is also possible to refer to multiple targets as once, \eg~to \cref{fig:onecol,fig:short-a}.
  You may also return to \cref{sec:formatting} or look at \cref{eq:also-important}.
\end{quotation}
```
If you do not wish to abbreviate the label, for example at the beginning of the sentence, you can use the
```latex
{\small\begin{verbatim}
  \Cref{...}
\end{verbatim}}
command. Here is an example:
\begin{quotation}
  \Cref{fig:onecol} is also quite important.
\end{quotation}
```

references.text:
## Problem Statement
The deployment of Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) in safety-critical domains (e.g., autonomous driving, face recognition) is hindered by their vulnerability to adversarial perturbations. To address this, we require **robustness verification**, which mathematically certifies that a model's output remains stable within a specific perturbation radius around an input.

While complete verifiers exist, they are NP-complete and computationally prohibitive for large networks. Consequently, the field relies on **incomplete verifiers** that use linear approximation (relaxation) to bound non-linear activation functions. However, a critical gap remains in the handling of the **MaxPool** function. MaxPool is a multivariate, non-linear function essential to CNNs, yet it is notoriously difficult to verify efficiently.

Current state-of-the-art approaches (e.g., DeepPoly, CNN-Cert) utilize coarse linear bounds that create large "over-approximation zones," leading to loose robustness certificates. Other methods attempt to transform MaxPool into sequences of ReLU and affine layers, but this introduces excessive computational overhead. Furthermore, recent "block-wise" tightest upper bounds are only optimal under restricted conditions (single upper linear constraints) and lose precision when combined with advanced Branch-and-Bound (BaB) techniques. We lack a verification framework that provides the **provably neuron-wise tightest** linear approximation for MaxPool without sacrificing computational efficiency.

## Core Hypothesis
We propose **Ti-Lin**, a novel robustness verification framework designed to minimize the over-approximation zone of MaxPool-based CNNs.

Our core hypothesis is that we can derive the mathematically **neuron-wise tightest** linear bounds for the MaxPool function by exploiting its piece-wise linear characteristics. Specifically, we hypothesize that the optimal upper linear bound is a hyperplane passing through specific endpoints of the space diagonal of the input region, while the optimal lower bound passes through the function value at the geometric center (midpoint) of the input bounds.

By minimizing the integral of the difference between the upper and lower linear bounds (the over-approximation volume), we expect to significantly tighten certified robustness bounds compared to existing relaxation techniques, while maintaining a low time complexity suitable for scalable verification.

## Proposed Methodology (Detailed Technical Approach)

We will develop a tight linear approximation method for the MaxPool function, $f(\mathbf{x}): \mathbb{R}^n \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$, defined as the maximum value within a pooling window. We assume the input vector $\mathbf{x} = (x_1, \dots, x_n)$ is bounded such that $x_i \in [l_i, u_i]$.

### 1. Mathematical Formulation of Linear Bounds
Our objective is to determine linear functions $l(\mathbf{x})$ and $u(\mathbf{x})$ such that:
$$ l(\mathbf{x}) \leq f(\mathbf{x}) \leq u(\mathbf{x}), \quad \forall \mathbf{x} \in [\mathbf{l}, \mathbf{u}] $$

We will construct these bounds to satisfy the **neuron-wise tightest** property, defined as minimizing the integral of the over-approximation error:
$$ \iint_{[\mathbf{l}, \mathbf{u}]} (u(\mathbf{x}) - l(\mathbf{x})) d\mathbf{x} $$

### 2. Construction of the Upper Linear Bound
To construct the upper bound $u(\mathbf{x}) = \sum a_i(x_i - l_i) + b$, we will identify key indices based on the input bounds. We will first sort the upper bounds $\{u_i\}$ to select the first ($i$), second ($j$), and third ($k$) largest elements. We will also identify $l_{max}$ as the largest element of $\{l_i\}$.

We propose a four-case formulation to determine the coefficients $a$ (slope) and $b$ (intercept) to ensure the plane passes through the optimal points on the convex hull of the MaxPool function:

*   **Case 1:** If $(l_i = l_{max}) \land (l_i \geq u_j)$:
    $$ a_i = 1; \quad b = l_i; \quad a_q = 0, \forall q \neq i $$
*   **Case 2:** If $(l_i = l_{max}) \land (u_j > l_i \geq u_k)$:
    $$ a_i = 1; \quad a_j = \frac{u_j - l_i}{u_j - l_j}; \quad b = l_i; \quad a_q = 0, \forall q \neq i, j $$
*   **Case 3:** If $(l_j = l_{max}) \land (l_i \neq l_{max}) \land (u_j \geq l_j \geq u_k)$:
    $$ a_i = \frac{u_i - l_j}{u_i - l_i}; \quad a_j = 1; \quad b = l_j; \quad a_q = 0, \forall q \neq i, j $$
*   **Case 4:** Otherwise:
    $$ a_i = \frac{u_i - u_k}{u_i - l_i}; \quad a_j = \frac{u_j - u_k}{u_j - l_j}; \quad b = u_k; \quad a_q = 0, \forall q \neq i, j $$

Geometrically, this construction ensures the upper bound plane passes through specific points $f(\mathbf{a})$ and $f(\mathbf{b})$, where $\mathbf{a}$ and $\mathbf{b}$ are the endpoints of the space diagonal of the input region defined by the indicator matrix of the active pooling inputs.

### 3. Construction of the Lower Linear Bound
For the lower bound, we will utilize the midpoint of the input intervals. Let us define the midpoint vector $\mathbf{m} \in \mathbb{R}^n$:
$$ m_i = \frac{l_i + u_i}{2}, \quad i = 1, \dots, n $$
We determine the index $q$ that maximizes this midpoint:
$$ q = \arg \max_i (m_i) $$
The lower linear bound will be defined as the value of the input at index $q$:
$$ l(x_1, \dots, x_n) = x_q $$
We will prove that selecting the variable with the maximum midpoint provides the neuron-wise tightest lower linear relaxation.

### 4. Algorithmic Implementation and Complexity
We will implement this logic into a modular verifier compatible with existing frameworks (e.g., DeepPoly, ERAN, $\alpha, \beta$-CROWN). The algorithm will require sorting the upper bounds to identify indices $i, j, k$, resulting in a time complexity of:
$$ \mathcal{O}(\text{pool\_size} \times \log 3) $$
This ensures that the computational cost remains negligible compared to the matrix multiplications in the linear layers, allowing for scalable verification of deep networks.

## Expected Contribution
1.  **Theoretical Advancement:** We expect to provide the first formal proof defining the **neuron-wise tightest** linear bounds for the multivariate MaxPool function, distinguishing our approach from block-wise approximations.
2.  **Minimization of Over-Approximation:** By mathematically minimizing the volume between $u(\mathbf{x})$ and $l(\mathbf{x})$, we anticipate significantly higher certified accuracy compared to state-of-the-art methods like DeepPoly and 3DCertify.
3.  **Efficiency:** The proposed method avoids the computational burden of transforming MaxPool layers into ReLU sequences (as done in OSIP), achieving tightening with negligible runtime overhead.
4.  **Versatility:** The formulation is general-purpose and will support various MaxPool-based architectures, including standard CNNs (LeNet, ResNet) and PointNets, against $l_1, l_2,$ and $l_\infty$ norm perturbations.

notes.model: claude-opus-5-5 through the Anthropic Messages API (llm.provider=anthropic), no fallback models, reviewer model = same model. Requests carry model, messages and max_tokens only (no tools, no thinking parameter); ARC's per-stage temperature is not sent because the model rejects it, so the API default applies.
notes.agent: ARC is not a tool-using coding agent: its 23-stage pipeline, its own code agent and its reviewers are prompt chains over plain chat completions. conditions.agent=claude means only that the provider is Anthropic; Claude Code is not involved. Generated experiments run as a plain subprocess in the container.
notes.effort: ARC has no effort setting; usage-log.patch sends output_config.effort='high' with every request. Haiku 5.5 thinks by default and ARC's per-stage max_tokens (for example 4096) is shared with the thinking tokens, so long outputs can still be cut short.
notes.venue: Not chosen by the system: export.target_conference=iclr_2026 comes from [systems.autoresearchclaw].
notes.tokens: ARC records no usage. A logging-only patch (usage-log.patch) appends each Messages API `usage` block to anthropic-usage.jsonl; cost is not computed. The same patch carries the RWE_OMIT_TEMPERATURE and RWE_EFFORT switches.
notes.time: No global wall-clock or budget cap in ARC; only the runner's limit applies. Per experiment run 3600 s, refinement iterations 10, repair cycles 3.
notes.input: Chinese pack text goes verbatim (candidate files concatenated, with <!-- file --> markers) into prompts.extra_prompts of 18 stages. ARC takes one topic string and checks generated code against it, so research.topic is the candidate TASK.md verbatim with whitespace collapsed. Literature queries come from the stage-3 model plan; ARC's ASCII keyword splitter and its whitespace-based query expansion yield a few useless queries from the Chinese text. Starter papers are guidance text only: ARC cannot ingest seed papers.
notes.search: Web search, crawling, GitHub, HF Hub, Gemini and OpenCode are off. Literature search in stage 4 uses ['openalex', 'semantic_scholar'] through ARC's own clients behind the shield proxy; stages 8, 17, 22 and 23 (novelty, citation verification) always also query arXiv, CrossRef and DataCite; the shield date-bounds those API calls like the others (a late DOI answers 403).
notes.server_side_search: Not reachable: every request to api.anthropic.com is built in researchclaw/llm/anthropic_adapter.py:136-148 and carries only model, messages, max_tokens, optional temperature, output_config.effort and system, never a tools or web_search field; the OpenAI-compatible client (OpenRouter :online / plugins) is not used (llm.provider=anthropic), web_search.enabled=false, Gemini is only used by the disabled figure_agent.nano_banana. Provider hosts are only tunnelled by the shield, so such a path would be invisible to the audit.
notes.secrets: Generated experiment code inherits the container environment, including the API keys (ARC offers no switch to scrub it).
notes.profile: project.profile=ml_generic is fixed for all tasks; research.domains is left empty because the literature screen rejects papers outside the stated domain (a theory task failed with domains=[machine-learning]).

notes.paper: The core writes a Markdown report (final_report.md); the EvoSkills paper-writing skill gives a generic LaTeX `article` skeleton with no ICML/ICLR/NeurIPS style and no compile step. The image has TeX Live (latexmk, fonts-extra) but no venue style files; the task asks for an official template, so a venue-formatted PDF depends on the agent obtaining the style through the shield. No extra pipeline stage was added; absent items are listed in result.missing.
notes.tools: skill_manager (git clone of any repository as a skill) is not registered (compat.patch); the Tavily key is not set so tavily_search does not exist; LANGGRAPH_CLI_NO_ANALYTICS=1; EvoSkills is baked in at its pinned commit. notes.limits: async sub-agents off (README advice for scripted runs); recursion_limit=1000000; model retry wait in auto-mode 1800 s (time without progress counts as wall time); execute timeout 300 s per command. No token or cost budget exists.

notes.model: Main agent, sub-agents and EvoScientist's auxiliary calls (tool selector, memory workers, summariser, graders) all use the configured model; auxiliary_model and model_fallbacks are empty.
notes.effort: Upstream hard-wires effort=max and max_tokens=128000 for Anthropic models. compat.patch makes the effort come from EVOSCIENTIST_REASONING_EFFORT (= conditions.effort); max_tokens stays 128000 (a cap, not a cost driver). Adaptive thinking (display=summarized) is upstream and not switchable.
notes.paper: The core writes a Markdown report (final_report.md); the EvoSkills paper-writing skill gives a generic LaTeX `article` skeleton with no ICML/ICLR/NeurIPS style and no compile step. The image has TeX Live (latexmk, fonts-extra) but no venue style files; the task asks for an official template, so a venue-formatted PDF depends on the agent obtaining the style through the shield. No extra pipeline stage was added; absent items are listed in result.missing.
notes.tools: skill_manager (git clone of any repository as a skill) is not registered (compat.patch); the Tavily key is not set so tavily_search does not exist; LANGGRAPH_CLI_NO_ANALYTICS=1; EvoSkills is baked in at its pinned commit. The execute shell and the EvoSkills paper-navigator scripts reach the world only through the shield; S2_DATE_CUTOFF is not set (the shield bounds dates).
notes.server_side_search: Not reachable: EvoScientist binds no provider-side search tool to any model (its only tools are think_tool, tavily_search when TAVILY_API_KEY is set, MCP tools from mcp.yaml, deepagents built-ins and skills; EvoScientist/EvoScientist.py:671-672 and 754-755 at the pin; the one bind_tools call is the tool selector's own output schema, middleware/tool_selector.py:166). TAVILY_API_KEY is not passed and the image has no mcp.yaml, so no search tool exists. Anthropic/OpenAI hosts are only tunnelled by the shield, so a provider-side search would be invisible to the audit.
notes.credentials: The provider key is in the process environment and EvoScientist's execute shell inherits the environment (upstream has no switch); the key is therefore visible to the agent's shell. It is a run-scoped copy and is not logged by this adapter.
notes.memory: A fresh data dir per run (baked skills, empty memory). Memory workers, skill synthesis and the scheduler stay at upstream defaults, so their LLM calls count in the usage log.
notes.limits: async sub-agents off (README advice for scripted runs); recursion_limit=1000000; model retry wait in auto-mode 1800 s (time without progress counts as wall time); execute timeout 300 s per command. No token or cost budget exists.
